text: Good morning, everyone.
Yeah. This morning I'd like to spend a few minutes talking about GBIF and
sustainability and how we approach it from
the secretariat and how we try to apply sustainable ideas.
I guess the bottom line is to see how we can bring in money and help
spread that money around to help us all out.
I guess the foundational thing about GBIF is we're an intergovernmental
organization celebrating our 25th year.
This is a picture from last year in Colombia.
Next week, we'll have our governing board here in Oslo.
We expect to have 120 people here next week, 33 voting
participants. So I
don't know of any other international organization such as ours who has 40
member countries that pay every year to the same biodiversity infrastructure.
And our funding from national investments has been flat and
slightly growing over the last five years. We have a governance mechanism.
We have the secretariat, in Copenhagen, and we have...
Oh, right in the middle of all that. That's a little scary, isn't it?
We have a governing board who I report to.
We have committees that we
give advice to the secretariat, and it all works quite well, and we'll have a nice
fun meeting next week discussing all that.
But one of the major things, as you all know about, is our peer-reviewed
publications using GBIF-mediated data.
This is really the core of
how GBIF works. This was done way before I got there.
A brilliant idea implemented. So you share data with GBIF,
we put DOIs on things coming in, going out, and we can track
how that data is used. And this is very
important to not only funders, the data producers, and the data
users. Here's a really good example.
This specimen was in an herbarium in Togo for a long time.
We received money in our first round of the BID program, Biodiversity Information
for Development.
Pierre Rageat, the herbarium director, was part of a grant that
mobilized this particular specimen.
That grant was come to us. This BID program is funded by the European Commission,
so if you're a European
taxpayer, your contribution helped this.
This specimen was shared
as part of that project, and then it was used in this
2023 paper by some Chinese authors
that cited it in a species distribution modeling.
And there are literally billions of examples of this, right?
Hundreds of millions of records are being used, eight peer-reviewed publications
every day and growing using GBIF data, and we can track all this.
It's just brilliant, and that really helps with the publication.
So the added layer to that is policy.
It's a bit more difficult to say specifically that
that specimen was used
in the IPBES report. But this is, of course, the 2023 IPBES
report was very important to our community, outlining the
billions of euros that
we waste in the world because of invasive species, right?
It's a huge,
not only financial, but of course, environmental impact of invasive species.
We did a citation tracking in that, looking at the papers that
were cited in this, because this uses secondary literature.
It doesn't do research itself, but it cites papers that do research.
31 of the 32 messages
in this report are
based or include GBIF-mediated data use in
peer-reviewed publications. So if you shared data before 2023,
it probably was cited in an IPBES report.
I double-checked with Daniel, this
exact paper was not used in the report because it was written in
2023 around the same time as this report.
So be assured
that if you're sharing data, it's being used for science and policy.
So as I mentioned, our financing is mainly by a
financial model that was put together in a memorandum of understanding.
It's renewed every five years, but it's based on GDP, so it's a fair
spreading out the contributions based on the ability of a country to pay.
So as I mentioned,
this has been flat or slowly growing over the last five years, but
we've been able to leverage this, and our budget actually
is twice as big as it was five years ago because we're leveraging
that stability
of these national contributions.
So our budget has doubled through contributions, through European Commission
grants, through foundations, special purpose funds, which some
of them are just actually large gifts that we can use as needed
to support our work program. And all of this goes straight into the work program to
support this. So I'll be telling the governing board next
week that they're getting a return on investment of 100%.
Every dollar they put in, they're getting €2.
I'll say it in euros tomorrow, next week.
But every euro that is contributed, there's €2 worth of work
program effort. And that, I think, we can keep growing.
But we don't want to be selfish as well because we do know that there is
lots of capacity. That's kind of a sad way of saying it, but there's lots of good
people who are underfunded and need funding to do your work, right?
And that's certainly true.
But we do have the ability to pass some of that on.
We, of course, have-- I hope you know of the CESS program,
Capacity Enhancement Support Program, which supports nodes in projects.
And we also have the BID program, which is our flagship program, which
this year we're funding. It's about a million euros worth of projects.
That's the money that will be spent this year around the world.
So in total,
approximately 25% of our budget is going
to activities here, either contractors that we support around the world
or projects or CESS projects in all six continents.
So we're spreading. So I'll tell the governing board next week,
for every euro you're spending, another euro is being
brought into the system, and 50% of that euro is actually going out the door to
support other projects.
And longer-term sustainability, we really focused on
driving this, and Libby kind of mentioned the
need to be important to policy. And for the past five years,
and even more so, but it's really coming to a head now, we've been driving
this relationship between data policy and funding.
We've developed a really good relationship with the Convention on Biological
Diversity and the Global Environment Facility,
World Bank, UNDP, these organizations that manage the
money that is used to do large-scale
conservation efforts around the world because they all need data, they all need
capacity, and what we do as a GBIF network enables that.
So this is something that is really coming to a head now with the start of
GEF 9, which is this new program of funds
that are coming out later this year, the Global Biodiversity Framework Fund,

And of course, many of you know the COP 17 next month.
We're really working closely with the

in these regional meetings.
So
this was a highlight for me last year.

more detailed use and explicit mention, recognition
